strengths: Introduces VisJudge-Bench, a large-scale benchmark (3,090 samples) covering single, multiple, and dashboard visualizations across 32 chart types, filling a gap in evaluating MLLMs for visualization quality.
Proposes a multi-dimensional evaluation framework (Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics) operationalized into six measurable dimensions, grounded in visualization theory.
Provides extensive evaluation of seven state-of-the-art MLLMs, revealing systematic gaps and biases (e.g., score inflation) compared to human experts.
Develops VisJudge, a specialized model fine-tuned with GRPO/LoRA, which significantly improves alignment with human judgments on the proposed test set.
Includes a three-stage annotation and quality control pipeline with crowdsourcing, validation checks, and expert adjudication, and addresses ethical considerations.
weaknesses: No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff’s alpha, ICC) are reported, making it difficult to assess the reliability of the human ground truth.
Evaluation lacks statistical significance tests and confidence intervals; reported differences between models may not be statistically significant.

Abstract and conclusion claim a 58.7% correlation improvement over GPT-5, but GPT-4o actually achieves the highest correlation among baselines (0.482), so the improvement over the best baseline is only 41.3%. This is misleading.
Potential train-test contamination: benchmark images are web-crawled and may appear in pretraining data of evaluated MLLMs, yet no analysis or mitigation is provided.
VisJudge is evaluated only on its own test set; no external validation on independent visualization quality datasets is provided to demonstrate generalization.
The specialized model training lacks ablations: no comparison to supervised fine-tuning, no ablation of reward components, no analysis of LoRA rank or GRPO hyperparameters.
The adaptive question generation using GPT-4o may introduce inconsistent or biased scoring criteria across samples; no analysis of generated criteria quality or prompt sensitivity is provided.
Data Fidelity is assessed only through visual inspection without access to underlying data, limiting the validity of fidelity claims.
Reproducibility concerns: the benchmark URL is missing, and details of GPT-4o filtering/classification and expert validation are insufficient for full replication.
Some references are incorrectly formatted or misattributed, and there are inconsistencies between main text and appendix (e.g., whether all samples received expert review).

strengths: Addresses an important gap: the lack of a systematic benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on visualization quality across fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics.
Introduces a large-scale dataset of 3,090 samples covering single visualizations, multiple visualizations, and dashboards across 32 chart types.
Proposes a multidimensional evaluation framework with six sub-dimensions grounded in visualization design principles.
Conducts extensive experiments with several representative MLLMs, including GPT-5, and provides a fine-tuned model (VisJudge) as a proof of concept.
Includes a detailed annotation pipeline with crowdsourcing, algorithmic quality control, and expert review.
Provides case studies and a scaling analysis that offer some practical insights into model behavior.
weaknesses: The reliability of the human ground truth is not established: no inter-annotator agreement (e.g., ICC, Krippendorff's alpha) is reported, so the human ceiling and noise level are unknown. This is critical for subjective aesthetic ratings.

The adaptive per-chart question and scoring criteria generated by GPT-4o make scores non-comparable across samples and introduce potential MLLM bias; the quality of these generated criteria is not validated.

Data Fidelity cannot be genuinely assessed without the original data. The benchmark only provides chart images, so annotators and models can only judge visual integrity or misleading design, not true data fidelity. This undermines a central claimed dimension.
Insight Discovery conflates data content with visualization quality. A well-designed chart of uninteresting data may be unfairly penalized, confounding design quality with dataset characteristics.

The model comparison is unfair: VisJudge is fine-tuned on 70% of the benchmark, while all baselines are evaluated zero-shot. No fine-tuned baseline or alternative training method (e.g., SFT, DPO) is compared.
There is no external validation. VisJudge and all baselines are evaluated only on the same benchmark, so generalization to unseen visualizations or other datasets is unknown.

No human ceiling or trivial baseline is reported. For a 1–5 scale with std 0.72, predicting the mean yields MAE ≈ 0.57, yet GPT-5 achieves only 0.551, barely better than a constant predictor. This suggests the benchmark may capture weak signal.
Evaluation metrics are not ideal: Pearson correlation is used on 1–5 ordinal ratings without Spearman/Kendall, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for model differences.

Reproducibility is limited: the benchmark link is omitted, code and model weights are not released, and the reported 70/10/20 split is inconsistent with the actual counts (2,163/279/648, i.e., ~70/9/21).

The expert review process is unclear: it is stated that all final scores were expert-determined, but later that only high-disagreement samples received expert attention. The actual coverage of expert review is not quantified.

Potential data contamination is not addressed: the dataset is web-crawled, so test images may have appeared in MLLM pretraining data, inflating baseline performance and undermining benchmark validity.

Training details are incomplete: no validation curves, no ablation of reward components, no comparison to standard SFT, and the scaling law is fit to few points without error bars or controls for compute.

The overall score MAE is much lower than the average per-dimension MAE (e.g., GPT-5: 0.551 vs ~0.74), likely due to averaging across dimensions. The paper emphasizes the overall metric, which may overstate per-dimension accuracy.

Ethical oversight is not documented: no IRB approval or informed consent details are provided for the crowdsourced human subjects, and the term 'expert-annotated' is misleading for largely crowd-sourced labels.

The writing and references contain numerous errors, inconsistencies, and typos (e.g., 'Research [2022] William S Cleveland...', mismatched years for Cao et al., misaligned author names), reducing clarity and professionalism.

strengths: Introduces the first comprehensive benchmark for MLLM visualization aesthetics and quality assessment, with 3,090 expert-annotated samples covering single visualizations, multiple visualizations, and dashboards across 32 chart types.
Provides a theoretically grounded multidimensional evaluation framework (Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics) with six sub-dimensions and an adaptive question generation mechanism.
Systematically evaluates seven representative MLLMs, revealing systematic biases such as score inflation and conservatism, and showing significant gaps between model and human expert judgments.
Proposes VisJudge, a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B model that substantially improves MAE and correlation over strong baselines, validating the benchmark as a useful training resource.
Offers detailed documentation of data collection, annotation workflow, quality control, prompts, and training configurations, supporting reproducibility.
Includes informative case studies, complexity analysis, and scaling analysis that provide useful insights into model behavior on visualization quality assessment.
weaknesses: Lacks inter-annotator agreement or human-human correlation metrics for the subjective quality scores, making it difficult to interpret model-human correlations (e.g., 0.681) and assess benchmark reliability.
The adaptive question and scoring criteria generation via GPT-4o is not validated; it may introduce variability, bias, or unfairness across charts and could affect construct validity.

The experimental setup reports vLLM for all inference, including proprietary models such as GPT-5, Claude, and Gemini, which is inconsistent and undermines reproducibility; no significance tests or confidence intervals are provided for model comparisons.

The test set (648 samples) is small for fine-grained subtype and dimension analyses (some subtypes have fewer than 10 samples), and many claims about model-specific strengths and hierarchical capabilities lack statistical support.
The specialized model VisJudge is trained with GRPO but lacks ablations against alternative fine-tuning methods (e.g., SFT, DPO) or reward designs, and no larger open-source baselines are included.
Potential ethical and legal concerns regarding web-scraped visualization images (copyright, licensing, attribution) are acknowledged but not sufficiently addressed for public release.
Novelty is moderate: existing visualization evaluation benchmarks already exist; the main advance is adding aesthetics, multi-view, and dashboard dimensions plus a fine-tuned model.

strengths: Introduces the first comprehensive benchmark for MLLM-based visualization aesthetics and quality assessment, with a multi-dimensional Fidelity/Expressiveness/Aesthetics framework covering single visualizations, multiple visualizations, and dashboards across 32 chart types.

Constructs a large-scale expert-annotated dataset of 3,090 samples with a detailed multi-stage annotation and quality-control pipeline, including crowdsourcing validation, conflict resolution, and expert adjudication, making it a potentially valuable community resource.

Systematically evaluates 12 representative MLLMs including GPT-5, revealing meaningful capability gaps and systematic biases such as score inflation, score concentration, and over-conservative judgments, with fine-grained analysis across dimensions and visualization types.

Proposes VisJudge, a domain-specific fine-tuned model using GRPO and LoRA, which consistently improves MAE and correlation across multiple backbone architectures and shows strong cross-architecture generalization.

Provides extensive additional experiments, case studies, data-scaling analysis, and real-world integration studies with MatPlotAgent and HAIChart, demonstrating practical utility beyond static benchmark evaluation.
The paper is generally well-organized and transparent about dataset construction, annotation protocols, training details, and planned release of data and model weights.
weaknesses: The reliability of the human ground truth is not fully established: no expert-expert agreement or human performance ceiling is reported, so it is unclear whether the claimed model-human gap and model improvements are meaningful relative to annotation noise. Crowd-expert MAE of roughly 0.54-0.59 on a 1-5 scale suggests non-trivial label uncertainty.

The Fidelity and Insight Discovery dimensions are assessed only from visual appearance because raw data are unavailable. This cannot verify true data fidelity or actual analytical insights, so claims about assessing data encoding accuracy and insight discovery are overstated; the benchmark should be framed as visual-level quality assessment.

Adaptive evaluation questions and scoring criteria are generated by GPT-4o, but the paper provides no systematic validation of the generated questions' quality, consistency, or metadata accuracy. This introduces potential bias and noise into both the human annotations and model evaluations.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, Pearson correlation is used on ordinal 1-5 ratings without Spearman/Kendall alternatives, and the 648-sample test set contains very small subtype groups (e.g., network graphs with n=5), limiting the strength of subtype-level conclusions.

The model contribution lacks key ablations: there is no supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline to isolate the benefit of GRPO, no ablation on reward components or LoRA configuration, and no comparison to rule-based or specialized visualization-quality scoring methods.

The real-world generalization study evaluates MatPlotAgent improvements using GPT-4o as the automatic evaluator, which is also one of the benchmarked models. This creates potential circularity or evaluator bias, and the reported HAIChart gains are modest and not tested for statistical significance.

The benchmark uses web-crawled images, but no contamination analysis is provided for closed-source MLLMs that may have seen these images during pretraining. Copyright/licensing details for released images are also thin, despite claims of compliance.

Some conceptual choices are debatable: rewarding design novelty/innovation may conflict with functional visualization quality, and aesthetic dimensions are inherently subjective. Without expert-expert agreement, the ground truth may partly reflect crowd preferences rather than a stable expert standard.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale expert-annotated benchmark (3,090 samples) covering single visualizations, multiple visualizations, and dashboards across 32 chart types, which is a useful resource for the visualization and MLLM communities.

Proposes a multi-dimensional evaluation framework (Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics) with six sub-dimensions, providing a structured way to assess visualization quality beyond simple chart understanding.
Conducts a broad empirical study of 12 representative MLLMs, revealing systematic biases such as score inflation and conservative scoring, which is informative for future model development.
Demonstrates that domain-specific fine-tuning (VisJudge) can improve alignment with human expert ratings, with substantial gains in MAE and correlation on the benchmark's test split.
Includes real-world application experiments on visualization generation (MatPlotAgent) and recommendation (HAIChart), showing potential practical utility of the learned evaluator.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction relies heavily on GPT-4o for metadata extraction and adaptive question generation; the human ground truth is conditioned on these generated questions, which may introduce bias and makes the benchmark less reproducible without the exact GPT-4o outputs.

The 'Data Fidelity' dimension is assessed without access to the underlying source data, so it only measures visual plausibility rather than true data accuracy, undermining a core claimed dimension of the framework.

Annotation quality analysis reports only mean absolute error (MAE) and does not provide standard inter-annotator agreement metrics (e.g., ICC, Krippendorff's alpha). A crowd-expert MAE of ~0.55 on a 1–5 scale is moderate and raises concerns about ground-truth reliability.

The expert validation process is described vaguely: three experts reviewing all 3,090 samples across six dimensions is an enormous workload, and details on their expertise, training, independence, and adjudication protocol are insufficient.

The main evaluation of VisJudge is in-domain: it is trained on 70% of the benchmark and tested on 20% of the same benchmark, so the large improvement over zero-shot baselines is expected and does not demonstrate generalization to unseen distributions.

The out-of-distribution experiments (MatPlotAgent, HAIChart) use GPT-4o as the automatic evaluator, which is itself a baseline model and may be biased toward outputs that align with its own preferences; no human validation of these OOD improvements is provided.

Missing ablations: no comparison to standard supervised fine-tuning, no ablation on the reward components, LoRA hyperparameters, or the adaptive question-generation strategy, making it difficult to attribute gains to specific design choices.
Results are reported without variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, despite running each model three times; this limits confidence in the reported differences.

The paper contains inconsistent reporting, e.g., the correlation improvement is stated as 60.5% over GPT-5 in the abstract/conclusion but 42.5% over GPT-4o in Section 5.2.1; Table 3 has confusing column headers, and several citations are incorrect or duplicated (e.g., Tufte misspelled, ArtiMuse attributed to multiple different references).

The claim of being the 'first comprehensive benchmark' is not sufficiently substantiated against closely related benchmarks such as VisEval, VIS-Shepherd, and chart QA benchmarks; the comparison table is high-level and omits important distinctions.
The model's generated rationales are not evaluated, even though they are part of the output format and claimed to be aligned with human expert judgments; only numeric scores are assessed.

The web-crawling data collection uses quality-modifier keywords (e.g., 'poor', 'confusing', 'professional'), which may introduce selection bias and may not reflect the natural distribution of real-world visualizations.
Ethical considerations around web-scraped data are mentioned but not thoroughly addressed; there is no detail on copyright clearance, licensing, or consent for the collected visualization images.

strengths: Addresses an important gap by proposing the first comprehensive benchmark for MLLM-based visualization aesthetics and quality assessment, spanning Fidelity, Expressiveness, and Aesthetics dimensions.

Constructs a large, diverse dataset of 3,090 real-world visualization samples across 32 chart types and three structural categories (single, multi-view, dashboards), with detailed subtype and domain distributions.
Employs a rigorous multi-stage annotation pipeline with crowdsourcing, automated quality control, and expert validation, and provides substantial analysis of annotation reliability and quality.

Systematically evaluates 12 representative MLLMs, including GPT-5 and open-source models, revealing systematic biases such as score inflation and limited discriminative ability on aesthetic dimensions.

Proposes VisJudge, a domain-specific fine-tuned model that substantially improves MAE and correlation with human expert scores across multiple backbone architectures, demonstrating cross-architecture generalization.

Validates practical utility through integration into visualization generation (MatPlotAgent) and recommendation (HAIChart) systems, showing consistent improvements over base models and commercial baselines.

Provides strong reproducibility signals by promising to release the benchmark, annotations, quality control records, and model weights, with extensive appendices detailing construction, prompts, and training.
Well-structured and clearly written, with informative case studies and error analyses that illustrate model failure modes.
weaknesses: The benchmark’s adaptive evaluation questions and scoring criteria are generated by GPT-4o, and human annotators scored samples using these generated rubrics. This introduces potential LLM-specific bias into the ground truth, and the validity of the generated rubrics is not independently established beyond expert score review.

Model evaluation relies on Pearson correlation for ordinal 1–5 scores; rank-based measures such as Spearman or Kendall would be more appropriate. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for model comparisons.

The Fidelity dimension is assessed only visually because raw data are unavailable for web-collected samples. This is acknowledged, but it limits objective verification of data faithfulness and may conflate visual encoding issues with actual data misrepresentation.

The fine-tuned VisJudge model is trained on the benchmark’s human scores and achieves MAE lower than the crowd-expert MAE, suggesting it may partially learn expert-specific annotation artifacts. Generalization is tested on only two downstream systems, so broader OOD robustness remains unclear.

The MatPlotAgent generalization experiment uses GPT-4o as an automatic evaluator, which may inherit the same biases the paper identifies in MLLM judges, weakening the strength of the reported generation improvements.

No comparison is made against existing non-MLLM visualization quality assessment or recommendation methods (e.g., rule-based or learning-based scorers) or against alternative fine-tuning strategies (e.g., SFT vs. GRPO) to isolate the source of improvement.

Inter-annotator agreement is reported mainly through MAE against expert scores rather than standard reliability metrics such as ICC or Krippendorff’s alpha, making it harder to assess the ceiling of achievable model performance.

Some claims, such as “first comprehensive benchmark,” are slightly strong given related visualization evaluation benchmarks, though the paper does differentiate its scope from chart QA, NL2VIS evaluation, and natural-image aesthetics benchmarks.
